I've been farming these 35 mu in Quzhou County for 40 years now. At 60 years old, with only myself in the household, I know exactly what I can and cannot do alone. Chrysanthemum is a good crop for me — the medicinal flower market has been steady, and buyers from the processing factories come right to the village. But it is labor‑intensive, especially at harvest when the flowers must be picked at just the right stage and dried quickly. With only my two hands, I have to hire workers for the heavy spells.

This year I will put all 35 mu into chrysanthemum. I have tried mixing in other crops before, but with one person managing the farm, keeping everything to one crop simplifies the labor scheduling and lets me focus on quality. I will rotary‑till the fields in early April to get a fine, loose seedbed — chrysanthemum roots need good aeration. I will plant improved seedlings around April 20th. I have used saved seed in the past, but the germination rate is uneven and I end up replanting gaps by hand, which wastes time I do not have. Improved seedlings cost about 300 yuan per mu, but they establish fast and give uniform stands.

For fertilizer, my experience says this soil is decent but tired after so many years of flowers. I will spread about 1,500 kg of chicken manure per mu as a basal dressing before planting — that is the foundation. Then I will put down 150 kg of 15‑15‑15 compound fertilizer at planting. When the plants start branching strongly in late May, I will topdress with 40 kg of urea per mu. That brings my nitrogen to roughly 40 kg per mu, phosphorus about 22 kg, and potassium about 22 kg. I split the nitrogen because one big dump early on makes the plants too leafy and they fall over in the autumn rains. I learned that the hard way three years ago.

Water comes from my well. I will irrigate four times: right after transplanting to help the seedlings settle, once at the branching stage in June if the spring turns dry, once when the buds are forming in August because that is when water demand spikes, and a last time during full bloom in late September if there is no rain. Pumping is not free — electricity for the well adds up — but skimping on water at budding means small flowers and the buyers downgrade my lot.

For crop protection, I will spray herbicide twice, once pre‑plant and once early post‑emergence, to keep the weeds down because hand‑weeding 35 mu alone is impossible. I will watch for aphids and leaf spot, which are the main problems here. If I see aphids building up, I spray insecticide — probably three times through the season. Fungicide for leaf spot, also about three times, especially after heavy rains. I do not spray on a rigid calendar; I walk the fields and look. But I budget for those eight applications because doing nothing risks losing the whole crop.

Labor is my biggest constraint. I will work about 120 days myself — managing, spraying, checking irrigation, and doing the light picking. But for transplanting, heavy weeding, and the main harvest, I need hired hands. I will hire roughly 100 days of labor this season: about 30 days for planting and early weeding, and 70 days for harvest and drying assistance. I pay 100 yuan per day for seasonal workers, so that is 10,000 yuan in wages I must set aside. I also need to keep some cash reserve for my own living expenses and for pumping costs.

I expect about 270 kg of dried flowers per mu if the autumn weather holds. Last year I got 275 kg, but there was a dry spell in August that stressed the plants slightly. I am aiming a little conservatively because at my age I would rather have a sure income than gamble on a record year.
